archetype.name: Rebuilding (year one of a new staff)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff under Mike LaFleur has a functional, ball-control offense but is still fielding the same leaky pass defense that sank the last regime, so the record is about what the play deserves.

report.headline: An honest 2-4: a competent offense paired with a secondary that keeps getting torched
report.take:
This Cardinals team is easy to misread from the standings. It is not a lucky 2-4 or an unlucky one. Wins over expected sit at 0.19 and the point differential implies 1.8 wins, so the record is almost exactly what the play has earned. That play splits into two very different halves. The offense, with Jacoby Brissett starting every week, is middling but sound: an 11th-ranked success rate, the 8th-best sack rate, the 2nd-fewest line penalties, and the 5th-most time of possession in the league. The defense is a different story. It ranks 28th in EPA allowed, and nearly all of that damage comes through the air.

The pass defense drives the season. Arizona is 30th in pass EPA allowed and 30th on deep throws, and opposing WR1s have produced more EPA per target against it than against any other defense. The yardage looks harmless, 11th in passing yards allowed a game, because the problem isn't steady gains. It's the explosive completion and the touchdown, about 2.67 passing scores allowed a game. A 25th-ranked pressure rate is the cause underneath it. Quarterbacks have time, and the coverage can't hold up that long. The run defense is genuinely good, 11th in rush EPA allowed and 5th in missed-tackle rate, which is why the losses look like shootouts rather than beatdowns on the ground.

Some of this needs context. Two of the ugliest defensive games came against San Francisco and Detroit, whose offenses now rank 2nd and 3rd. The best win, 26-14 at the Chargers, came against the league's 32nd-ranked offense. History says the leak is not a fluke, though. Defensive EPA allowed was 0.087 last season and 0.091 in 2023, nearly identical to now, so this is a roster-level problem the new staff inherited. The offense also hides a weakness: run success is decent at 12th, but a 25th-ranked stuff rate and 3.49 yards a carry show a line that loses at the point of attack, with the 4th-best short-yardage conversion rate covering for it.

The outlook is a team that keeps games closer than last year's 3-14 squad did but loses most of them to better passing attacks. The back half of the schedule has plenty of beatable opponents and several bad defenses, which gives the offense room to win some games outright. Unless the pass rush finds another gear, expect a season in the five-to-seven-win range, built on time of possession and enough points to outlast weaker teams.

strengths.title: An offense that stays on schedule
strengths.body: Arizona doesn't generate many explosive plays, but it rarely loses downs. An 11th-ranked success rate, an 8th-ranked sack rate and almost no line penalties keep drives alive, and that is where the 5th-ranked time of possession comes from. It's a repeatable formula because it rests on protection and discipline rather than turnover luck.

strengths.title: Stout, sure-tackling run defense
strengths.body: The front holds up against the run: 11th in rush EPA allowed, 5th in missed-tackle rate, and lead backs held below their usual production. It forces opponents to beat Arizona through the air. That's cold comfort given the secondary, but it is a real foundation and it won't erode.

strengths.title: McBride as the engine
strengths.body: Trey McBride has drawn 65 targets, the most on the team, ahead of Michael Wilson's 58. A tight end at the center of a short-area, keep-the-chains-moving passing game suits Brissett's profile and gives the offense a dependable read on money downs.

concerns.title: Deep passes and top receivers feast
concerns.body: This is the defining flaw. Arizona ranks 30th in pass EPA allowed and 30th on deep balls, and the WR1 matchup is the worst in the league by EPA per target. It was nearly as bad in 2025 and 2023, so it is structural rather than a small-sample blip. Facing elite offenses like San Francisco and Detroit inflated the numbers some, but not enough to explain them away.

concerns.title: Too little pressure up front
concerns.body: A 16.5% pressure rate ranks 25th, and that is the root of the coverage problems: quarterbacks get time to wait for routes to come open downfield. The sack total is respectable at 14, so the rush finishes when it gets home, but it doesn't get home often. Without a scheme or personnel change, this persists.

concerns.title: Run blocking loses at the line
concerns.body: Arizona's backs are getting hit early: a 24% stuff rate ranks 25th, yards before contact ranks 22nd and the team averages 3.49 yards a carry. The strong short-yardage rate shows the line can win when it fires off on a known run, but on early downs the ground game is a drag, and the backfield is thin with Jeremiyah Love hurt and James Conner still on IR.

trend.note: Arizona opened with an upset at the Chargers, lost three straight with blowouts by Seattle and Detroit, then stole an 18-16 win in Los Angeles as a 12.5-point underdog. Passing EPA has swung from +10.1 at San Francisco to -18.2 at the Giants, so there is no steady line to draw yet.

nextGame.headline: Denver's shaky 4-2 comes to town missing two secondary starters
nextGame.body:
Denver's 4-2 record is shakier than Arizona's 2-4 is misleading. The Broncos have a negative point differential and a 21st-ranked margin a game, have won every one-score game, and lead the league in takeaways. The offense underneath is weak: 24th in EPA, 28th in success rate, 31st in yards a game. Their defense is excellent against the pass, 3rd in pass EPA allowed with the 3rd-most sacks, but soft on the ground, 26th in rush EPA allowed, 28th in explosive runs allowed and dead last in missed-tackle rate. Opponents already lean on the run against Denver, and Arizona should too. Meanwhile Arizona's worst unit, its pass defense, draws a below-average passing offense led by Bo Nix, who has started every game. The Book has Denver by 4.5 with a 43.5 total, which frames this as a low-scoring game decided by a play or two.

Availability tilts toward Arizona on one side and against it on the other. Denver is without cornerback Pat Surtain II and safety Talanoa Hufanga, two of its most-used defenders, which weakens the very pass defense that carries the team. Arizona is thin at safety too, with Andrew Wingard and Wydett Williams Jr. both out, a worry for a unit that already gives up the deep ball. Jeremiyah Love is listed out with his ankle, though LaFleur said he was expected to do some running; if he can't go, Tyler Allgeier carries the load, and James Conner isn't expected to have his return window opened this week.

waysToWin.title: Run Allgeier into Denver's soft front
waysToWin.body: Denver is 26th against the run by EPA, gives up explosive runs and misses more tackles than any defense. Even with Arizona's blocking problems, steady carries keep Brissett out of obvious passing downs against a strong pass rush and play to Arizona's time-of-possession style. This edge is real for Denver all season, not a fluke.

waysToWin.title: Hit the depleted secondary through McBride
waysToWin.body: With Surtain and Hufanga out, Denver's top-3 pass defense is missing two key pieces. Arizona's offense runs through McBride, and Denver has allowed 0.44 EPA a target to opposing tight ends, 27th in the league. Brissett's protection, 8th in sack rate, gives him a chance to work the middle.

waysToWin.title: Squeeze a punchless offense
waysToWin.body: Denver averages 254 yards a game, 31st, and ranks 28th in success rate, so this is the rare opponent that may not punish Arizona's coverage. If the run defense holds as usual and Arizona controls the clock, the Broncos may not have enough possessions to lean on their one-score luck.

waysToLose.title: Feeding the league's top takeaway defense
waysToLose.body: Denver's record rests on turnovers: 11 takeaways, most in the league. Arizona's one game with three giveaways, at the Giants, became a 12-point loss despite four sacks by the defense. In a game with a total this low, two turnovers likely decide it.

waysToLose.title: Nix finds the deep ball
waysToLose.body: Even a weak passing offense can hit the shots Arizona keeps allowing. Arizona is 30th on deep throws and worst in the league against WR1s, and it plays without two safeties. A couple of explosive completions could hand Denver the points its offense otherwise struggles to produce.

waysToLose.title: Pass rush wrecks obvious passing downs
waysToLose.body: If Arizona's run game stalls and it falls behind the chains, Denver's rush takes over: 18 sacks, 3rd in the league, and the 3rd-best QB hit rate. Detroit got to Brissett five times. Long-yardage situations are where this game slips away.

nextGame.watch: Arizona's early-down run calls. If Allgeier, or Love if he is cleared, can punish Denver's 26th-ranked run defense, Brissett stays out of the Broncos' pass rush and this becomes Arizona's kind of grinding game.

restOfSeason.body:
Nothing about this record is luck-driven, so there is no big regression coming in either direction. The turnover differential is even, one-score results are a coin flip, and wins over expected is near zero. What changes is the opposition. After Kansas City, Seattle and a closing game against San Francisco, the schedule is full of 2-4 and worse teams, and Dallas, New Orleans, Washington and Philadelphia all field bottom-eight defenses by EPA. Arizona's stay-on-schedule offense should score more against those units than it did against Seattle's 2nd-ranked defense.

The pass defense is the cap. It has been bad for three of the last four seasons, and without more pressure the 30th-ranked coverage numbers will improve only as the quarterbacks get worse. Expect points allowed to drift down somewhat as the schedule softens, but not to league average. The run game could get a lift if Love's ankle heals and Conner returns from IR, which matters because the line is not creating much on its own.
swingFactors: Whether the pass rush can lift its 25th-ranked pressure rate
Health of the backfield: Love's ankle and Conner's return from IR
Turnovers against a soft back-half schedule

confidence.note: Six games is a small sample, but the record matches the efficiency and the defensive profile matches the last several seasons.
